rv.q: This is a musical that hits all the right spots, achieving something close to Broadway grace.
The musical adaptation of the hit 1992 movie about a lounge singer who hides out in a convent is a blessed event, a crowd-pleasing entertainment that manages to be both reverent and irreverent.
The musical is a crowd-pleaser that delivers exactly what it promises — a feel-good evening of uplifting songs, dancing nuns and broadly drawn comedy.
It looks penuriously designed, possibly by Paul Ryan, and it’s lit like a Baghdad suburb.
Despite the ministrations of these shtickmeisters the show remains tame, innocuous and frankly a little dull.
This musical adaptation is a crowd-pleaser that delivers exactly what you'd expect.
To people who love this show that will be many, cheerful entertainment is the point.

After a rocky gestation that included a 17-month West End run and the recent addition of Beane and replacement director Jerry Zaks, the Broadway version of “Sister Act” is glossy, but seems like a worn set of tires repatched too often.
The musical takes a good 1992 big-screen comedy starring Whoopi Goldberg, one of the show’s producers, and makes it better.
It's a pleasure to find that "Sister Act," a new adaptation of the 1992. Whoopi Goldberg film comedy, is energetic, hilarious and thoroughly enjoyable.
And now there's "Sister Act," a lively and extremely funny musical comedy with an infectious score of new disco numbers
It's delivered with exceptional glee and polish.
Let's just say it's hard to resist when the sisters and a few brothers make such a joyful noise.
It's all good fun and, in the end, not bad theology either.
It has its own distinct and surprising charms.
And you watch a lot of the show smiling despite yourself.
Also, God, please forgive Alan Menken for having to replace the film’s pop music with original songs, which did make me tap my toes during a recent press performance.

Another problem, for which Zaks is perhaps most at fault, is that the musical’s tone is neither a satire of the Catholic Church nor all that respectful of the institution, which leads to a troubling superficiality.
A ramshackle yet agreeable film comedy with plausibility issues has here become an even more ramshackle and outlandish musical comedy that consistently diminishes its source.

A genial musical that has no intention but to entertain, which it does expertly and enthusiastically, “Sister Act” is a cinch with the summertime tourist crowd and likely to please many a local customer.

There’s fun, if not musical comedy heaven, to be found in Sister Act, the new Broadway musical adaptation of the hit 1992 movie starring Whoopi Goldberg. Featuring plenty of talent both on and off stage, the show boasts some terrific performances, an engaging ‘70s era-style soul-flavored score, and a few raucous laughs.

cn.t: Critics find this musical adaptation an energetic, crowd-pleasing entertainment with strong performances and infectious disco numbers, though some dismiss it as silly and cartoonish with juvenile humor that doesn't transcend its formulaic origins.

sg.ra: The Broadway Theatre is a 1924 column-free house — Wikipedia notes the balcony is carried by a 40-ton girder 'supported solely by the side walls,' which eliminates the pillar problems that plague older big Shubert houses of this size. That makes center orchestra D-G genuinely safer than at most 1,700+ seat theatres: no interior posts to work around. Multiple guides converge on rows D-G, seats 105-109, as the premium sweet spot, and center orchestra row G seat 105 was reviewed simply as 'Center orchestra. What could be better?'. Caveat for this specific house: the orchestra pit sits between row A and the stage, and reviewers consistently report the stage is unusually high — front-row patrons 'can't see feet' and crane their neck. D-G hits the first row where eyeline clears cleanly, well ahead of the mezzanine overhang at row J-K.

sg.n: Orchestra Left / Right Mid (Rows C-L, side blocks)
sg.ra: The Broadway Theatre's orchestra side blocks (Left even-numbered, Right odd-numbered) sit at a sharp angle because the house is unusually wide — 46'6" proscenium in a ~909-seat orchestra. Far-aisle seats past double-digits (14+) get the worst of the angle: one Gatsby reviewer in Orchestra L row B seat 10 warned 'restricted view, missed basically all action at the back of the stage, as well as the grandeur of the set itself.' The mid-range (rows C-L, seats up to low teens) is a real $50-cheaper alternative to center — Orchestra L row E seat 2: 'This seat is like $50 cheaper than center orchestra. You can still see everything and since you're on the aisle you don't have to worry about a head getting in the way.' Row E is called out specifically as close enough for facial expressions with no obstruction.

This is the single most-warned-about zone at the Broadway Theatre because of its unusual geometry: above you sits the cantilevered 1675 Broadway office tower, and the mezzanine overhang drops hard over the rear orchestra. Per AViewFromMySeat Orchestra R row U seat 13: 'theres a bit of a balcony overhang that blocks the view at the top of the stage.' Row T's own SneakyBeagle agreed. One Miss Saigon reviewer in Orchestra R row T seat 23 was blunt: 'felt very far back, mezzanine overhang gave an odd feeling of separation from the action onstage. Would recommend a closer seat or something in the mezzanine.' In a house this size, the smarter move is a rear-mezzanine row A-B at similar price — you get elevation instead of being crushed under the overhang.

The Broadway Theatre's front mezzanine is the smallest section in the house (only 250 seats across 6 rows A-F) and sits very close to the stage because the single-balcony construction means no upper balcony above it — 'No overhang from Rear Mezzanine' per SeatPlan, a structural feature you don't get in most big Broadway houses with two-tier balconies. Reviewers repeatedly call Front Mezz LC/RC A-C 'some of the best seats in this theatre' (AbbeySouth44), and for spectacle shows with vertical staging the overhead angle is actively preferred — a West Side Story reviewer specifically said 'Best to see this show in Mezz to see video portion of the set. Front orchestra would miss action.' The row A safety railing can cut into sightlines for shorter patrons so row B is the safer pick.

Front Mezz L/R at the Broadway Theatre is the sleeper-comfort pick in the building because of one very specific quirk: the far ends of row A 'flare out' where the row meets the aisle, creating outsized legroom. An AVFMS reviewer in Front Mezzanine L row A seat 16 says it plainly: 'This seat probably has the most legroom in the whole theatre! Because it's on the edge of the row where it flares out, you can fully straighten your legs! The lefthand corner of the stage is slightly obscured by the railing, but it's so worth it.' Trade-off is a slightly cut stage-corner and the usual side angle, but for 6'+ patrons in a house whose mid-rows are repeatedly called 'tight', this is an actual workaround rather than a marketing claim.

Rear Mezzanine Center row A-C is the Broadway Theatre's signature value play because of a layout feature specific to this house: the rear mezzanine is 'elevated above the Front Mezzanine' with a horizontal aisle dividing the two, and row A of the rear mezz has that aisle directly in front — so no heads block sightlines in the first rear-mezz row. AViewFromMySeat user in RC row A seat 111 confirmed: 'theres an aisle in front of the seats so no heads are in front of you.' Combined with the column-free engineering, center-A is an unobstructed elevated center-perspective at rear-mezz prices — one 123LGB reviewer: 'Looks far in the photo but it felt closer. Good sightlines.' Caveats: one 6'2" reviewer called RC row A seat 111 'agony' — railing sits at knee height — so book further back if you're tall.

Rear Mezzanine at the Broadway Theatre runs A-R (an unusually deep balcony — 584 seats alone, larger than many full Broadway houses), and SeatPlan warns views become 'less reliable' beyond row J with the back quarter feeling 'very distant.' Side blocks (Rear Mezzanine L, Rear Mezzanine R rows E-R) compound distance with angle — one Great Gatsby reviewer in Rear Mezzanine LC row E seat 122 confirmed 'Good view of the stage, but was very far away,' and E seat 11 reviewer: 'No obstructions though you do feel the distance between the stage. Cannot see facial expressions.' In a house already 900+ seats deep in the orchestra, combining side-angle with deep balcony distance is the worst combination of hazards offered here.
